danish.title: Anden bog (1805) — Kapitel 19
paragraphs: Det sjette jægerregiments angreb sikrede tilbagetrækningen af vores højre fløj. I midten forsinkede Tushins glemte batteri, som var lykkedes med at sætte ild til landsbyen Schön Grabern, den franske fremrykning. Franskmændene slukkede den brand, som vinden bredte, og gav os derved tid til at trække os tilbage. Tilbagetrækningen af midten til den anden side af sænkningen bagved var forhastet og støjende, men de enkelte kompagnier blev ikke blandet sammen. Men vores venstre fløj — der bestod af Azov- og Podolsk-infanteriet og Pavlograd-husarerne — blev samtidig angrebet og omgået af overlegne franske styrker under Lannes og kastet i forvirring. Bagration havde sendt Zjerkov til generalen, der kommanderede venstre fløj, med ordre om straks at trække sig tilbage.

Zjerkov, der ikke tog hånden fra huen, drejede sin hest og galopperede af sted. Men så snart han havde forladt Bagration, svigtede modet ham. Han blev grebet af panik og kunne ikke ride derhen, hvor det var farligt.
Da han nåede venstre fløj, ledte han i stedet for at ride frem, hvor der blev skudt, efter generalen og hans stab, hvor de umuligt kunne befinde sig, og afleverede derfor ikke ordren.

Kommandoen over venstre fløj tilhørte ifølge anciennitet kommandøren for det regiment, som Kutuzov havde inspiceret ved Braunau, og i hvilket Dolokhov tjente som menig. Men kommandoen over den yderste venstre fløj var blevet overdraget til kommandøren for Pavlograd-regimentet, hvor Rostov tjente, og der opstod en misforståelse. De to kommandører var yderst opbragte på hinanden, og længe efter at kampen var begyndt på højre fløj, og franskmændene allerede rykkede frem, var de stadig optaget af en diskussion, hvis eneste formål var at fornærme hinanden. Men regimenterne, både kavaleri og infanteri, var på ingen måde rede til den forestående kamp. Fra menig til general ventede ingen et slag og var optaget af fredelige sysler — kavaleriet fodrede hestene og infanteriet samlede brænde.

»Han er højere i rang end jeg,« sagde den tyske oberst for husarerne med rødmende ansigt til en adjutant, der var redet op, »så lad ham gøre, hvad han vil, men jeg kan ikke ofre mine husarer... Hornblæser, blæs til retræte!«

Men hast var ved at blive bydende nødvendig. Kanon- og geværild tordnede til højre og i midten, mens Lannes' skarpskytters kapper allerede var at se, idet de krydsede mølledæmningen og formerede sig inden for dobbelt muskettrækkens afstand. Infanterigeneralen gik hen mod sin hest med rykvise skridt, og da han var kommet op, rettede han sig i hele sin højde og red hen til Pavlograd-kommandøren. De to kommandører mødtes med høflige buk, men med hemmelig ondskab i hjertet.
»Endnu en gang, oberst,« sagde generalen, »kan jeg ikke efterlade halvdelen af mine folk i skoven. Jeg beder Dem, jeg beder Dem,« gentog han, »om at indtage stillingen og forberede et angreb.«
»Og jeg beder Dem om ikke at blande Dem i, hvad der ikke vedkommer Dem!« svarede den opbragte oberst pludselig. »Hvis De var ved kavaleriet...«
»Jeg er ikke ved kavaleriet, oberst, men jeg er en russisk general, og hvis De ikke er klar over det...«

»Fuldstændig klar over det, Deres excellence!« råbte obersten pludselig, idet han rørte sin hest og blev purpurrød i ansigtet. »Vær så venlig at ride frem og se, at denne stilling er ubrugelig! Jeg agter ikke at lade mine folk gå til grunde for Deres fornøjelses skyld!«
»De glemmer Dem selv, oberst. Jeg tager ikke hensyn til min egen fornøjelse, og jeg vil ikke tillade, at man siger det!«

Generalen, der opfattede oberstens udbrud som en udfordring af hans mod, rettede brystet og red med rynkede bryn ved siden af ham til frontlinjen, som om deres uenighed ville blive afgjort dér midt iblandt kuglerne. De nåede fronten; adskillige kugler susede over dem, og de holdt stille i tavshed. Der var intet nyt at se fra linjen, for allerede fra det sted, hvor de havde befundet sig før, havde det været tydeligt, at kavaleriet umuligt kunne operere mellem buskene og det ujævne terræn, og at franskmændene omgik vores venstre fløj. Generalen og obersten stirrede strengt og betydningsfuldt på hinanden som to kamphaner, der gør sig rede til kamp, idet de forgæves forsøgte at opdage tegn på fejhed hos den anden. Begge bestod prøven. Da der ikke var noget at sige, og ingen af dem ønskede at give anledning til den påstand, at han havde været den første til at forlade kugleregnen, ville de have stået der i lang tid og prøvet hinandens mod, hvis det ikke havde været for, at de netop da hørte raslen af geværild og et dæmpet råb næsten bag dem i skoven. Franskmændene havde angrebet de soldater, der samlede brænde i krattet. Det var ikke længere muligt for husarerne at trække sig tilbage med infanteriet. De var afskåret fra tilbagetogsvejen til venstre af franskmændene. Hvor ubekvem stillingen end var, måtte de nu angribe for at bane sig vej ud.

Eskadronen, hvori Rostov tjente, havde næppe fået tid til at sidde op, før den blev standset med front mod fjenden. Igen, som ved Enns-broen, var der intet mellem eskadronen og fjenden, og igen lå den forfærdelige skillelinje af uvished og frygt — lig den linje, der adskiller de levende fra de døde — imellem dem. Alle følte denne usynlige linje, og spørgsmålet om, hvorvidt de ville krydse den eller ej, og hvordan de ville krydse den, optog dem alle.

Obersten red frem til fronten, gav vredt et svar på spørgsmål fra officererne, og som en mand der desperat insisterer på at få sin vilje, gav en ordre. Ingen sagde noget bestemt, men rygtet om et angreb bredte sig gennem eskadronen. Kommandoen til at formere lød, og sablerne hvislede, da de blev trukket af skeden. Stadig rørte ingen sig. Tropperne på den venstre fløj, infanteri og husarer i lige grad, mærkede, at kommandøren selv ikke vidste, hvad han skulle gøre, og denne ubeslutsomhed smittede af på folkene.
»Bare de ville skynde sig!« tænkte Rostov og følte, at tiden endelig var kommet til at opleve den angrebets glæde, han så ofte havde hørt om fra sine kammerater.
»Fremad, med Guds hjælp, gutter!« lød Denisovs stemme. »I trav, fremad!«
Hestenes kryds begyndte at gynge i den forreste linje. Rook (Rostovs hest) trak i tøjlerne og satte af sig selv i gang.
Foran sig, til højre, så Rostov frontlinjen af sine husarer og endnu længere fremme en mørk linje, som han ikke tydeligt kunne se, men antog for fjenden. Skud hørtes, men et stykke borte.
»Hurtigere!« lød kommandoen, og Rostov mærkede Rooks flanker synke, da hesten gik i galop.

Rostov foregreb sin hests bevægelser og blev mere og mere begejstret. Han havde bemærket et ensomt træ foran sig. Dette træ havde været midt i den linje, der havde virket så forfærdelig — og nu havde han krydset den linje, og ikke blot var der intet forfærdeligt, men alt blev mere og mere muntert og livligt. »Åh, hvor vil jeg hugge løs på ham!« tænkte Rostov, idet han greb sabelgrebets hæfte.

»Hurra-a-a-ah!« brusede et råb af stemmer. »Lad bare nogen komme i min vej nu,« tænkte Rostov, idet han drev sporerne i Rook og lod ham gå i fuld galop, så han overhalede de andre. Forude var fjenden allerede synlig. Pludselig fejede noget som en birkekost hen over eskadronen. Rostov hævede sablen, klar til at hugge, men i det øjeblik fór tropper Nikitenko, der galopperede forude, fra ham, og Rostov følte som i en drøm, at han fortsat blev ført fremad med unaturlig fart, men dog blev på samme sted. Bagfra stødte Bondartjuk, en husar han kendte, mod ham og så vredt på ham. Bondartjuks hest slog et sving og galopperede forbi.

»Hvorfor rykker jeg ikke fremad? Jeg er faldet, jeg er dræbt!« spurgte og besvarede Rostov i samme øjeblik. Han var alene midt på en mark. I stedet for heste i bevægelse og husarers rygge så han intet foran sig end den ubevægelige jord og stubben omkring ham. Der var varmt blod under hans arm. »Nej, jeg er såret, og hesten er dræbt.« Rook forsøgte at rejse sig på forbenene, men faldt tilbage og fastholdt sin rytters ben. Blod strømmede fra hestens hoved; den kæmpede, men kunne ikke rejse sig. Rostov forsøgte ligeledes at rejse sig, men faldt tilbage, da hans sabeltaske var viklet ind i sadlen. Hvor vores folk var, og hvor franskmændene, vidste han ikke. Der var ingen i nærheden.

Da han havde fået benet fri, rejste han sig. »Hvor, på hvilken side var nu den linje, der så skarpt havde adskilt de to hære?« spurgte han sig selv og kunne ikke svare. »Kan noget slemt være hændt mig?« undrede han sig, idet han kom på benene; og i det øjeblik følte han, at noget overflødigt hang på hans følelsesløse venstre arm. Håndleddet føltes, som var det ikke hans. Han undersøgte sin hånd omhyggeligt og ledte forgæves efter blod. »Ah, dér kommer folk,« tænkte han glad, da han så nogle mænd løbe mod ham. »De vil hjælpe mig!« Forrest kom en mand i en underlig tsjako og en blå kappe, mørk, solbrændt og med en kroget næse. Så kom to mere, og mange flere løb bagefter. Én af dem sagde noget mærkeligt, ikke på russisk. Blandt de bageste af disse mænd i ens tsjakoer var en russisk husar. Han blev holdt fast om armene, og hans hest blev trukket bagved.

»Det må være en af vores, en fange. Ja. Kan det være, at de også tager mig? Hvem er de her folk?« tænkte Rostov, der næppe troede sine egne øjne. »Kan de være franskmænd?« Han så på de nærmende franskmænd, og skønt han blot et øjeblik forinden havde galopperet for at nå dem og hugge dem ned, syntes deres nærhed nu så frygtelig, at han ikke kunne tro sine øjne. »Hvem er de? Hvorfor løber de? Kan det være, de kommer efter mig? Og hvorfor? For at dræbe mig? Mig, som alle er så glade for?« Han mindedes sin moders kærlighed til ham, sin families og sine venners, og fjendens hensigt om at dræbe ham syntes umulig. »Men måske gør de det alligevel!« I mere end ti sekunder stod han uden at røre sig af stedet eller fatte situationen. Den forreste franskand, ham med den krogede næse, var allerede så tæt på, at man kunne se udtrykket i hans ansigt. Og det ophidsede, fremmede ansigt på den mand, hans bajonet der hang ned, hans tilbageholdte åndedræt og hans lette løb skræmte Rostov. Han greb sin pistol og kastede den i stedet for at affyre den mod franskanden og løb af alle kræfter mod buskene. Han løb nu ikke med den tvivl og indre kamp, han havde følt på Enns-broen, men med følelsen af en hare, der flygter fra hundene. Én eneste fornemmelse, frygten for sit unge og lykkelige liv, beherskede hele hans væsen. Han sprang hurtigt over furerne og flygtede over marken med den fart, han plejede at vise i fangeleg, og nu og da vendte han sit godmodige, blege, unge ansigt for at se bagud. Et gys af rædsel gennemfor ham: »Nej, hellere lade være med at se,« tænkte han, men da han havde nået buskene, så han sig om endnu en gang. Franskmændene var faldet bagud, og netop som han kiggede, satte den forreste mand farten ned til gang og vendte sig om og råbte noget højt til en kammerat længere bagved. Rostov standsede. »Nej, det må være en fejltagelse,« tænkte han. »De kan umuligt have villet dræbe mig.« Men samtidig føltes hans venstre arm, som om der var bundet en halvtreds kilos vægt til den. Han kunne ikke løbe mere. Franskanden standsede også og sigtede. Rostov lukkede øjnene og dukkede sig. En kugle og så en til susede forbi ham. Han samlede sine sidste kræfter, greb sin venstre hånd med den højre og nåede buskene. Bag dem var der russiske skarpskytter.

english.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter 19
paragraphs: The attack by the Sixth Chasseurs secured the retreat of the right flank. In the center, Tushin's forgotten battery—which had managed to set fire to the village of Schon Grabern—held up the French advance. The French were busy putting out the fire, which the wind kept spreading, and that bought the Russians time to pull back. The retreat of the center behind the ravine was rushed and noisy, but at least the different companies didn't get jumbled together. The left flank, however—made up of the Azov and Podolsk infantry regiments and the Pavlograd hussars—was simultaneously attacked and outflanked by superior French forces under Lannes and thrown into chaos. Bagration had sent Zherkov to the general commanding the left flank with orders to retreat immediately.

Zherkov, keeping his hand at his cap, wheeled his horse around and galloped off. But the moment he left Bagration's side, his nerve failed him. Panic seized him, and he simply could not go where it was dangerous.

When he reached the left flank, instead of riding to the front where the firing was, he went looking for the general and his staff in places where they couldn't possibly be. And so the order was never delivered.

Command of the left flank belonged by seniority to the colonel of the regiment Kutuzov had reviewed at Braunau—the one where Dolokhov was serving as a private. But command of the extreme left had been given to the colonel of the Pavlograd hussars, Rostov's regiment, and a bitter misunderstanding erupted between the two commanders. They were thoroughly infuriated with each other and, long after the fighting had begun on the right and the French were already advancing, they were still locked in a quarrel whose only real purpose was to insult one another. Meanwhile, their regiments—cavalry and infantry alike—were completely unprepared for battle. From privates to generals, nobody was expecting a fight. They were all engaged in peaceful activities: the cavalry feeding their horses, the infantry gathering firewood.

"He is higher in rank zan I am," said the German colonel of the hussars, his face flushing, to an adjutant who had ridden up. "So let him do vhat he vill, but I cannot sacrifice my hussars. Bugler, sound ze retreat!"

But there was no more time to waste. Cannon and musket fire, blending together, thundered on the right and in the center, while the long coats of Lannes's sharpshooters were already visible crossing the mill dam and forming up within twice a musket shot's range. The infantry general walked over to his horse with jerky steps, mounted up, drew himself very straight and tall, and rode over to the Pavlograd colonel. The two commanders met with polite bows, barely concealing the hostility in their hearts.
"Once again, Colonel," said the general, "I cannot leave half my men behind in the woods. I'm asking you—I'm begging you—to take up your position and prepare to attack."
"And I am begging you not to interfere in vhat is not your affair!" the colonel suddenly snapped. "If you vere cavalry..."
"I am not cavalry, Colonel, but I am a Russian general, and if you don't know that..."

"I know it perfectly vell, your excellency!" the colonel suddenly shouted, spurring his horse forward, his face going purple. "Vill you be so kind as to come to ze front and see for yourself zat zis position is no good? I vill not destroy my men for your pleasure!"
"You forget yourself, Colonel! I am not considering my own pleasure, and I won't have anyone say that I am!"

Taking the colonel's outburst as a challenge to his courage, the general puffed out his chest and rode beside him toward the front line, scowling, as if the dispute could be settled right there among the flying bullets. They reached the line, several rounds whizzed past them, and they stopped in silence. There was nothing new to see from there—it had already been obvious from further back that cavalry couldn't operate among the bushes and broken terrain, and that the French were outflanking the left. The general and the colonel stared at each other sternly and significantly, like two fighting cocks before a match, each trying to detect signs of cowardice in the other. Both passed the test. Since there was nothing to say, and neither man wanted to be the first to leave the zone of fire and give the other grounds to accuse him, they might have stood there indefinitely, testing each other's nerve—had they not heard, just then, the rattle of musket fire and muffled shouting almost behind them, in the woods. The French had attacked the men gathering firewood in the copse. It was no longer possible for the hussars to retreat with the infantry. They were cut off from their line of retreat on the left by the French. However bad the position was, the only option now was to attack—to cut a way through.

Rostov's squadron barely had time to mount before it was halted, facing the enemy. Once again, as at the bridge over the Enns, there was nothing between the squadron and the enemy, and once again that terrible, invisible line of uncertainty and fear—the line between the living and the dead—lay between them. Everyone felt it, and the question of whether they would cross it, and how, filled them all with dread.

The colonel rode to the front, angrily snapped at the officers' questions, and—like a man desperately determined to have his way—gave an order. Nobody said anything specific, but the rumor of an attack rippled through the squadron. The command to form up rang out. Sabers whistled as they slid from their scabbards. Still, no one moved. The troops on the left flank, hussars and infantry alike, could sense that their commander didn't know what to do himself, and his uncertainty spread to every man.
"If only they'd hurry!" thought Rostov, feeling that the moment had finally come for the kind of glorious charge he'd heard his fellow hussars describe so many times.
"Fo'ward, with God, lads!" rang out Denisov's voice. "At a t-wot, fo'ward!"
The horses' hindquarters began to sway in the front rank. Rook tugged at his reins and broke into motion on his own.

To his right, ahead of him, Rostov could see the front line of his hussars and, further off, a dark line he couldn't quite make out but assumed was the enemy. Shots were audible, though still some distance away.
"Faster!" came the command, and Rostov felt Rook's flanks drop as the horse broke into a gallop.

Rostov anticipated his horse's every movement and felt more exhilarated by the second. He'd fixed his eyes on a lone tree ahead. That tree had been in the middle of the line that had seemed so terrifying—and now he'd crossed it, and not only was there nothing terrible, but everything was becoming more thrilling, more alive. "Oh, how I'll cut at him!" thought Rostov, gripping the hilt of his saber.

"Hurrah!" roared the voices around him. "Just let someone come at me now," thought Rostov, driving his spurs into Rook and urging him to a full gallop until he outpaced the rest. The enemy was visible ahead. Then suddenly something like a birch broom seemed to sweep across the squadron. Rostov raised his saber to strike—but at that instant the trooper Nikitenko, who'd been galloping just ahead, shot away from him, and Rostov felt, as in a dream, that he was being carried forward at an impossible speed yet somehow staying in the same spot. Behind him, Bondarchuk, a hussar he knew, crashed into him and glared angrily. Bondarchuk's horse swerved and galloped past.

"Why aren't I moving? I've fallen. I'm killed!" Rostov asked himself and answered in the same breath. He was alone in the middle of a field. Instead of galloping horses and hussars' backs, all he could see was the motionless earth and stubble around him. Something warm and wet spread under his arm. "No—I'm wounded, and the horse is killed." Rook tried to push himself up on his front legs but fell back, pinning his rider's leg. Blood poured from the horse's head; he thrashed but couldn't stand. Rostov tried to rise too but fell back—his sabretache had gotten tangled in the saddle. Where the Russians were, where the French were, he had no idea. There was nobody near.

Having freed his leg, he stood up. "Where is the line now—that line that had so sharply divided the two armies?" he asked himself, and couldn't answer. "Has something terrible happened to me?" he wondered as he got to his feet. At that moment he felt something extra hanging from his numb left arm. His wrist felt like it belonged to someone else. He examined his hand carefully, searching in vain for blood. "Ah, here come some people," he thought with a rush of joy, seeing men running toward him. "They'll help me!" The first man wore a strange-looking shako and a blue cloak; he was swarthy, sunburned, with a hooked nose. Then came two more, and many more behind them. One of them said something in a language that wasn't Russian. Among the men at the back, wearing the same unfamiliar shakos, was a Russian hussar being held by the arms, his horse led behind him.

"It must be one of ours—a prisoner. Wait... Could they actually take me prisoner too? Who are these men?" thought Rostov, barely believing his eyes. "Can they be French?" He stared at the approaching Frenchmen, and though just a moment before he'd been galloping straight at them with every intention of hacking them to pieces, their nearness now felt so horrifying that he couldn't trust his own eyes. "Who are they? Why are they running? Can they be coming for me? And why? To kill me? Me—whom everyone loves?" He thought of his mother's love, his family's love, his friends' love, and the idea that these strangers wanted to kill him seemed impossible. "But maybe they actually will." For more than ten seconds he stood rooted to the spot, unable to comprehend what was happening. The first Frenchman, the hook-nosed one, was now so close that Rostov could read the expression on his face. And the sight of that excited, foreign face—the man's bayonet lowered, holding his breath, running so lightly—terrified Rostov. He grabbed his pistol and, instead of firing it, hurled it at the Frenchman and ran for the bushes with everything he had. He no longer ran with the doubt and inner conflict he'd felt crossing the bridge at Enns. He ran with the instinct of a hare fleeing hounds. One single feeling possessed him completely: fear for his young, happy life. Bounding over furrows, he sprinted across the field with the same desperate speed he'd once shown playing tag, turning now and then to glance back with his kind, pale, young face. A shudder of terror ran through him: "No, don't look back," he thought, but when he reached the bushes he looked around one more time. The French had fallen behind, and just as he turned, the first man slowed from a run to a walk, turned, and shouted something to a comrade further back. Rostov stopped. "No, this is some kind of mistake," he thought. "They can't really want to kill me." But at the same time his left arm felt as if a seventy-pound weight were tied to it. He couldn't run anymore. The Frenchman stopped too and took aim. Rostov squeezed his eyes shut and ducked. One bullet, then another, whistled past him. He gathered his last remaining strength, grabbed his left hand with his right, and reached the bushes. Behind them were Russian sharpshooters.
